title: Block Cipher Modes
subtitle: ECB, CBC, CTR, GCM — why mode choice matters

whyItExists.problem: AES can only encrypt exactly 16 bytes at a time. Real messages are longer. How you chain those 16-byte operations determines the security properties of the final scheme.
whyItExists.solution: Modes of operation define how to chain block cipher calls. Different modes provide different security properties: some provide only confidentiality (CBC, CTR), others provide both confidentiality and integrity (GCM, CCM).
whyItExists.whenToUse: AES-GCM for new code. AES-CTR when you need a stream cipher without authentication. AES-CBC only for legacy compatibility.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: ECB mode — ever. CBC mode for new code (no authentication). CTR alone without an authentication tag.

explainModes.beginner: Imagine AES as a 16-byte box. Modes are instructions for how to handle a long message: cut it into 16-byte pieces and scramble them in different ways.
explainModes.simple: ECB scrambles each piece independently (bad — identical pieces look identical). CBC links pieces together (better). GCM links them and also checks for tampering (best).
explainModes.standard: ECB (never use), CBC (encryption only, padding oracle risk), CTR (stream mode, parallelisable), GCM (AEAD: confidentiality + integrity). Always use GCM for new code.
explainModes.technical: ECB: each block encrypted independently with same key → deterministic, pattern-leaking. CBC: each block XORed with previous ciphertext before encryption → sequential, needs padding. CTR: keystream generated by encrypting an incrementing counter, XORed with plaintext → stream cipher, no padding. GCM: CTR mode + GHASH authentication over ciphertext and AAD.
explainModes.deepDive: GCM uses GHASH, a universal hash over GF(2^128), to compute the authentication tag. The tag covers both the AAD and the ciphertext, binding them together. Nonce-misuse resistant variants (AES-GCM-SIV) are safer when nonce uniqueness is hard to guarantee.

content.text: AES is a 16-byte block cipher. To encrypt messages longer than 16 bytes, you need a mode of operation. The mode determines how blocks are chained and what security properties you get. Choosing the wrong mode is a common source of real-world vulnerabilities.
ECB encrypts each 16-byte block independently with the same key. The result: identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks. This leaks patterns catastrophically.

content.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes
import os

key = os.urandom(32)

# ECB — illustrating WHY it's broken
# A 32-byte message with repeated 16-byte blocks
message = b"YELLOW SUBMARINE" * 2  # two identical blocks

cipher = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.ECB())
enc = cipher.encryptor()
ciphertext = enc.update(message) + enc.finalize()

# The two halves of ciphertext are IDENTICAL!
print(ciphertext[:16].hex())
print(ciphertext[16:].hex())
# Output: same line twice — the structure of the data leaks through

# This is why the 'ECB penguin' demo exists:
# encrypting a bitmap with ECB still shows the original image outline

content.text: Never use ECB mode in production. It is demonstrably broken. If you encrypt an image in ECB mode, you can still see the shapes (the famous 'ECB penguin'). No real algorithm should ever default to ECB.

CBC fixes ECB by XORing each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting. The first block is XORed with an IV (Initialisation Vector). This makes each ciphertext block dependent on all previous blocks.

content.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import padding as sym_padding
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
import os

key = os.urandom(32)
message = b"Secret data that must stay private"

# --- CBC: encryption only (no authentication) ---
iv = os.urandom(16)
padder = sym_padding.PKCS7(128).padder()
padded_msg = padder.update(message) + padder.finalize()

cipher = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CBC(iv))
enc = cipher.encryptor()
cbc_ciphertext = enc.update(padded_msg) + enc.finalize()
print("CBC ciphertext:", cbc_ciphertext.hex())
# CBC has no way to detect if ciphertext was modified!

# --- GCM: encryption + authentication (AEAD) ---
gcm_key = AESGCM.generate_key(256)
nonce = os.urandom(12)
aesgcm = AESGCM(gcm_key)
gcm_ciphertext = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, message, None)
print("GCM ciphertext:", gcm_ciphertext.hex())
# Flip a byte in ciphertext — decryption will raise InvalidTag

a.name: AES-CBC
a.description: Block mode with IV; sequential; needs padding

content.code:
Mode | Confidentiality | Authentication | Parallelisable | Use
-----|-----------------|----------------|----------------|----
ECB  | BROKEN          | No             | Yes            | NEVER
CBC  | Yes             | No             | Decrypt only   | Legacy
CTR  | Yes             | No             | Yes            | Streaming (add MAC separately)
CCM  | Yes             | Yes (AEAD)     | No             | IoT/constrained devices
GCM  | Yes             | Yes (AEAD)     | Yes            | RECOMMENDED for new code
SIV  | Yes             | Yes (AEAD)     | Partial        | When nonce uniqueness is hard

content.text: When in doubt: use AESGCM from the cryptography library with a random 12-byte nonce. It handles padding, authentication, and cipher chaining correctly in one call.

questions.question: Why should you never use ECB mode?
options: It is too slow for modern hardware
Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, leaking data patterns
questions.explanation: ECB encrypts each block independently. Two identical 16-byte blocks produce identical ciphertext — the structure of the data is visible.

questions.question: What is a padding oracle attack?
options: An attack where the attacker guesses the encryption key
An attack that exploits AES-CBC padding error responses to decrypt ciphertext byte by byte
An attack on the IV generation process
An attack that requires physical access to the hardware
questions.explanation: In AES-CBC with PKCS7 padding, if a server distinguishes padding errors from other errors, an attacker can use that oracle to decrypt arbitrary ciphertext one byte at a time.

questions.question: Which mode provides BOTH confidentiality and integrity in a single operation?
questions.explanation: GCM is an AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) mode. It encrypts the data AND generates an authentication tag that detects tampering.

faq.q: What is a padding oracle attack?
faq.a: An attack on AES-CBC where an attacker modifies ciphertext and observes whether the server returns a 'padding error'. By repeating this, the attacker can decrypt any ciphertext byte by byte without the key. The fix is to use authenticated encryption (GCM) so modified ciphertext is rejected before padding is checked.

A famous demonstration where a bitmap image of a Linux penguin (Tux) is encrypted with AES-ECB. The resulting ciphertext still shows the outline of the penguin because identical pixel blocks encrypt to identical ciphertext blocks.
Only if you separately add an authentication MAC (HMAC-SHA256) over the ciphertext. This is called 'Encrypt-then-MAC'. It is easier and safer to just use AES-GCM, which does both automatically.

examples: The BEAST attack (2011) exploited AES-CBC's predictable IV in TLS 1.0, allowing decryption of cookies
The POODLE attack (2014) used CBC padding oracles to attack SSL 3.0, forcing browsers to disable SSLv3
TLS 1.3 eliminated CBC-based cipher suites entirely, requiring AEAD (GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305)
